questionText: A pair of fair dice is thrown repeatedly until a sum of 7 appears. The probability that the experiment terminates in at most 3 throws is:

options.mistakeAnalysis: Aspirants compute $1/6 = 36/216$.
Aspirants report the probability of failure in all 3 throws $q^3 = 125/216$.
Aspirants assume a 50% termination chance.
Correct answer. $P(\text{sum } 7) = 1/6 \implies q = 5/6$. Probability $= 1 - q^3 = 1 - (5/6)^3 = 1 - 125/216 = 91/216$.

detailedSolution:
When rolling two dice, total outcomes $= 36$.
A sum of 7 occurs for pairs: $\{(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)\}$ (6 outcomes).
Probability of success on any throw: $p = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}$.
Probability of failure: $q = 1 - p = \frac{5}{6}$.
The experiment terminates in at most 3 throws if success occurs on the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd throw, which is the complement of failing all 3 throws:
$P(\le 3\text{ throws}) = 1 - P(\text{failing all 3 throws}) = 1 - q^3 = 1 - \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^3 = 1 - \frac{125}{216} = \frac{216 - 125}{216} = \frac{91}{216}$.

questionText: The function $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ defined by $f(n) = \begin{cases} \frac{n + 1}{2}, & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \\ \frac{n}{2}, & \text{if } n \text{ is even} \end{cases}$ is:

options.mistakeAnalysis: Aspirants assume piecewise parity formulas are always bijective.
Aspirants fail to verify that all natural numbers are covered in the range.
Correct answer. $f(1) = 1$ and $f(2) = 1$ (not one-one); every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ has an even pre-image $n = 2k$ (onto).

detailedSolution:
1. Injectivity: Consider $n = 1$ (odd) and $n = 2$ (even):
$f(1) = \frac{1 + 1}{2} = 1$
$f(2) = \frac{2}{2} = 1$.
Since $f(1) = f(2)$ while $1 \ne 2$, the function is not one-one.
2. Surjectivity: For any arbitrary $k \in \mathbb{N}$, consider the even integer $n = 2k \in \mathbb{N}$:
$f(2k) = \frac{2k}{2} = k$.
Thus, every element $k$ in the codomain $\mathbb{N}$ has a pre-image in the domain $\mathbb{N}$. Hence, $f$ is onto.
Therefore, $f$ is onto but not one-one.

questionText: If $A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $A^{4} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ k & 1\end{bmatrix}$, then the value of $k$ is:

options.mistakeAnalysis: Aspirants compute $3^3 = 27$.
Aspirants multiply $3 \times 12 = 36$.
Correct answer. Lower triangular matrix powers satisfy $A^n = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3n & 1\end{bmatrix}$. For $n=4$, $k = 3(4) = 12$.

Calculate successive powers of $A$:
$A^2 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3+3 & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 6 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
$A^3 = A^2 A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 6 & 1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 9 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
By induction, $A^n = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3n & 1\end{bmatrix}$.
For $n = 4$:
$A^4 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3(4) & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 12 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.
Equating with $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ k & 1\end{bmatrix}$, we get $k = 12$.
